notes.meaning: Jesus walked away from the crowded house in Capernaum and sat down by the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Sitting by the cool water gave Him a restful place to be while letting people gather around Him.

The crowds pressed in so closely that Jesus stepped into a small boat and pushed out onto the water. Sitting in the boat was the usual posture of an authoritative Jewish teacher. This gave Him breathing room and allowed His voice to carry clearly to all the people standing on the beach.

Jesus began teaching the crowd through parables, which are earthly stories that illustrate heavenly truths. He pictured a familiar Galilean farmer walking across a field, scattering seed by hand over the ground.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom noted that the farmer scatters seed freely on every kind of soil without favoritism, showing that God desires all people to hear.

notes.meaning: In Bible times, footpaths ran right through and around the edges of plowed fields. Some seeds fell on this hard, beaten ground where they could not sink into the soil, and hungry birds quickly flew down and ate them up.

In many fields in Israel, flat limestone rock sits just beneath a thin layer of soil. Seeds that fell here sprouted very quickly because the shallow earth warmed up fast in the sun, even though the rock gave the roots no space to grow downward.

When the morning sun rose high and beat down with intense heat, the young plants were quickly scorched. Because they had no deep roots to draw up moisture from the dry ground, they quickly withered away and died.

Other seeds fell into soil where thorn bushes had been cut away, but their roots remained hidden under the surface. As the crop sprouted, the stubborn weeds grew up faster and stronger, blocking the sunlight and choking out the grain.

Some seed fell on deep, plowed ground that had been cleared of rocks and weeds. This fertile earth allowed the grain to grow fully and produce a rich harvest, though individual plants yielded different amounts, such as a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom observed that the varied harvests show God's mercy, because He welcomes different measures of obedience rather than requiring only one high standard.

notes.meaning: Jesus urged everyone who had ears to pay close and serious attention to what He had said. This was a common call to look beyond the surface of the story and seek out its true spiritual meaning.

The disciples came to Jesus privately in the boat and asked why He was suddenly speaking to the crowds in parables. They were surprised by this new way of teaching, which hid the plain truth from casual listeners.

Jesus explained that God had granted His disciples the privilege of understanding the hidden truths of the kingdom of heaven. In Scripture, a mystery is not an impossible puzzle, but a divine secret that God chooses to reveal to His followers while keeping it veiled from those who reject Him.

differ.view: Reformed Christians teach that God sovereignly chooses to grant spiritual understanding and saving faith only to the elect.
Methodists teach that God gives understanding according to whether people freely value, improve, and obey the light they have received.

notes.meaning: This is a divine principle about spiritual growth: whoever values and obeys God's truth will be given even greater understanding and grace. But anyone who ignores or wastes what God has shown them will end up losing even the little light they once possessed.

differ.view: Here the saying mainly praises God's kindness. He keeps adding to what He has begun in His own people. In Matthew 25 the same words are used about the right use of gifts.
"Whoever has" means whoever puts God's grace to use. This is God's fixed rule in dealing with everyone.

notes.meaning: Jesus taught in parables because the people had watched His miracles and heard His preaching, yet stubbornly refused to believe. Telling these stories showed both judgment on their willing blindness and mercy to curious seekers who might be prompted to search deeper.

Jesus stated that the people's unbelief fulfilled the words of the prophet Isaiah. The people had hardened their own hearts, covered their ears, and shut their eyes against God's light, fearing that turning to Him would require them to repent and let Him heal their spiritual sickness.

Jesus declared His disciples truly blessed because their spiritual eyes and ears were open to God's truth. While the crowds turned away, the disciples recognized the light of the gospel and were eager to learn from their Lord.

Old Testament prophets and faithful believers had looked forward to the coming Messiah, catching only glimpses of God's future kingdom from afar. The disciples were far more privileged, as they were living in the very days of fulfillment, hearing Jesus preach and watching Him work.

Jesus called on His disciples to pay close attention as He explained the meaning of the sower. Since they were given ears to hear, He wanted them to understand clearly how God's message is received in different human hearts.

The seed that fell along the hard path represents a person who hears the gospel but pays no real attention to it. Because the heart is hardened and unresponsive, Satan quickly comes like a hungry bird and snatches the message away before it can sink in.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: John Chrysostom taught that people can change the condition of their hearts, and that losing the word depends on their own choice rather than an unchangeable nature.

notes.meaning: The rocky ground represents someone who receives the gospel with great joy and excitement, but has no deep roots of repentance. Because there is no lasting commitment to Christ, the person quickly abandons the faith as soon as trouble or persecution begins.

differ.view: Reformed Christians view this hearer as having only a temporary, outward show of faith without ever being truly regenerated.
Methodists believe this hearer experienced a genuine start in God's grace and joy, but genuinely fell away through lack of enduring faith.

notes.meaning: The thorny ground represents a hearer who accepts the message, but allows competing desires to crowd it out. Everyday anxieties, the struggles of life, and the false promise of wealth strangle spiritual growth until the person produces no fruit for God.

differ.view: True faith, planted by God's Spirit, can never be lost. So those who fall away only seemed to believe.
This hearer did have root and was in large part changed inside. Yet the thorns slowly choked the word until it bore no fruit.

notes.meaning: The good soil represents someone who hears the message of the kingdom, takes it to heart, and holds firmly to it. Such a person lives a fruitful life of faithful obedience, though each believer yields varying amounts of fruit according to their circumstances and gifts.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern critics think the explanation in verses 18-23 reads the story with too much detail. They doubt it is exactly what Jesus first said.

notes.meaning: Jesus told another parable to explain what the kingdom of heaven is like during the present age. In this story, a landowner planted clean, healthy wheat seed across his field, representing Christ sowing true believers and His truth into the world.

While the farmhands were sleeping at night, an enemy came and scattered darnel among the freshly sown wheat. Darnel is a poisonous weed that looks almost identical to wheat in its early stages, picturing the subtle way Satan introduces false believers and deceptive ideas among God's people.

As the crop grew through the season, the difference between the two plants stayed hidden. But once the stalks formed heads of grain, the counterfeit darnel became obvious, showing that genuine faith is ultimately recognized by its spiritual fruit.

The owner's servants were shocked to discover weeds spreading across the field and asked where they had come from. Their question reflects the deep distress faithful believers feel when corruption and hypocrisy appear within the church.

The landowner explained that an enemy had done the damage, assuring his servants that the bad seed was not part of his own design. When the servants offered to rush out and pull up the weeds, they displayed an eager human desire to wipe out evil immediately.

The landowner told the servants to wait because the roots of the darnel and wheat were intertwined beneath the ground, and pulling the weeds would destroy the good grain. Jesus taught His followers that God alone will carry out the final separation of good and bad at the harvest, warning against hasty human efforts to root people out.
